notes: Revision 2: desk and field rules now carry hour values for the countdown (desk 3-4 h, limited evidence; field 1 h fueling interval during hikes >1 h, moderate evidence in athletes). The 'any' rule stays null by design. Hour values are app guidance derived from the cited per-dose / per-hour recommendations, not validated cutoffs.
disclaimer: General wellness information, not medical advice. Evidence on meal frequency is mixed; athlete-derived fueling guidance is applied to strenuous hikes.

countdown.basis: app translation of the ISSN 'every 3-4 h' protein-spacing recommendation

rules.notes: Countdown: next meal or snack due 3 h after the last one, and try not to go past 4 h while awake. Basis: the ISSN protein position stand (Jäger 2017) and nutrient-timing stand (Kerksick 2017) recommend spreading protein doses (~0.25 g/kg, 20-40 g) evenly every 3-4 h; this comes from studies in exercising/resistance-trained adults, so for a desk day it is an extrapolation (evidence: limited). Three meals plus one snack across a ~14-16 h waking day also works out to roughly every 3-4 h, which supports regular eating for someone who tends to undereat. The AHA scientific statement (St-Onge 2017) does NOT set an interval: it reports that skipping breakfast and irregular meals are associated with worse cardiometabolic markers, mostly from observational studies, and that trials on meal frequency are mixed (limited evidence). Protein target: DGA 2025-2030 1.2-1.6 g/kg/day (~110-145 g/day). Intermittent fasting or time-restricted eating is NOT recommended here: trials show no added weight or metabolic benefit over regular calorie-matched eating in most people (Lowe 2020; Liu 2022), and it works against eating enough. The hours are app guidance, not a validated cutoff.

rules.notes: Countdown on field days: every 1 h DURING hikes longer than ~1 h (fueling.intervalHours). Thomas 2016 (AND/DC/ACSM joint position) gives carbohydrate per hour by duration: <45 min not needed; 45-75 min small amounts; 1-2.5 h 30-60 g/h; >2.5-3 h up to 90 g/h. It gives grams per hour, not an eating interval; 'every hour' is the app's translation (small amounts more often are equally fine). maxHoursBetween is null because the guideline sets no upper gap; the hourly countdown already covers it. Before/after the hike, use the desk spacing (offHikeMinHoursBetween 3 / offHikeMaxHoursBetween 4, limited evidence, see desk rule) if the app knows hike start/end; otherwise the 1 h countdown applies all day, which errs toward eating more. Pre-hike: a carbohydrate-containing meal 1-4 h before, 1-4 g carbohydrate/kg (~91-363 g for 90.7 kg). After: carbohydrate plus ~0.25-0.3 g/kg protein (~23-27 g) within ~2 h (Thomas 2016; Jäger 2017). Evidence is from athletes; strenuous hiking is a reasonable but not identical application (moderate). snacksPerDay is null because it depends on hike length.

rules.notes: Fallback rule with no hour values on purpose: no guideline sets a universal meal interval for adults (AHA 2017: evidence on meal frequency/timing is limited and mixed), so the app should use the desk or field rule, or the user's own reminder interval. Chrononutrition: some small trials suggest earlier eating windows improve insulin sensitivity (Sutton 2018: 8 men with prediabetes, 5 weeks), but this is preliminary (limited evidence) and is not a recommendation here. Perishable packed foods should not sit unrefrigerated for >2 h (>1 h above 90°F) per USDA FSIS; pack a cooler/ice pack or choose 'no-cooler' snacks on field days.

hydration.notes: National Academies Adequate Intake for men 19+: 3.7 L/day TOTAL water (beverages + food moisture), of which ~3.0 L (about 13 cups) from beverages. This is an Adequate Intake (population median), not a precise requirement; needs rise with heat and activity. Bach-Faig 2011 suggests 1.5-2 L/day of water as the main drink.

hydration.notes: About 0.4-0.8 L per hour during exercise, adjusted for heat, terrain and individual sweat rate (ACSM 2016). Goal: avoid losing >2% of body weight (~1.8 kg for 90.7 kg) without over-drinking (over-drinking beyond sweat losses risks hyponatremia). A single number is not supported because sweat rates vary widely; weigh yourself before/after hikes to learn your rate. For long or very sweaty hikes, drinks/foods containing sodium help (ACSM 2007 suggests ~20-30 mEq/L sodium in fluids for prolonged exercise); DGA 2025-2030 notes highly active people may need more than 2,300 mg sodium/day.
